timeline.story: In 2014, Remy played ordinary household games, sometimes following a sibling’s plan and sometimes making up their own. No single activity occupied most afternoons, and family memories do not identify an early specialist interest.

At six, they began school and enjoyed some days more than others. During 2017, they tried the activities available in class without deciding that any one task described them especially well or needed to continue at home.

In 2018, Remy completed ordinary reading, drawing, mathematics, and group assignments. Some were easier to start than others, but they did not build a distinctive project history, and adults generally accepted that preferences could remain unsettled.

During 2020, they followed the household’s changing school routine with help when needed. Familiar people mattered, while many descriptions of adult work still sounded abstract because Remy had not visited the settings or seen the everyday tasks involved.

At twelve, Remy found it difficult to answer questions about future plans beyond saying they might stay nearby. In 2023, they continued regular classes without joining a club, starting paid work, or arranging a shadowing experience.

Across 2024 and 2025, classmates became more definite about their plans, but Remy still could not picture most activities well enough to judge them. Several new settings sounded worth seeing, without prompting a particular creative project or professional identity.

At sixteen in 2026, Remy wants supportive introductions to Texas college and training settings and time to revisit first impressions. A close-to-home future with low spending is only an initial sketch; uncertainty currently describes missing experience rather than a conclusion about capacity.

Everyday essentials cover phone, home supplies, health, and any saved debt or care costs. These are editable estimates, not price quotes. Home and car purchases also take upfront money. Phone, household, and health costs are included; existing debt and care needs are kept. The income range estimates 2026 employee taxes and retirement saving, then adds room to leave 20% of take-home unallocated at the upper end. It is a budget target range, not an income ceiling or a probability.
